issues.legal_issue: A dying declaration recorded by a magistrate may be relied on despite the non-examination of the doctor who was present, and may alone support a conviction when the magistrate verified the declarant’s ability to make the statement and the declaration is reliable.
material_facts: The magistrate recorded the injured person’s statement within hours of his hospital admission and testified that he had checked the person’s consciousness and ability to make the statement by asking preliminary questions.
A doctor was present and endorsed that the injured person was conscious, but the doctor was not examined at trial.
The declaration implicated the accused and contained relevant details of the incident; the Court found no suspicious feature affecting its credibility.
The declaration did not mention the accused’s lip injury, which the injured person may not have had an opportunity to observe.
issues.conclusion: The magistrate-recorded dying declaration was reliable despite the doctor’s non-examination and could form the sole basis for a conviction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the settled principle that a reliable dying declaration can by itself support a conviction. Under Laxman v. State of Maharashtra, the absence of a doctor’s certification that the declarant was in a fit state of mind is not fatal where the magistrate is satisfied of that fitness; the contrary proposition in P. Rosamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh was no longer good law. Relying on State of Maharashtra v. Krishnamurti, the Court also held that omission to mention injuries to the accused does not require rejection where the declarant may not have been able to observe them.

predicates.dying_declaration_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction that rests on a dying declaration.
predicates.declaration_recorded_by_magistrate: A magistrate recorded the injured person’s statement as a dying declaration.
predicates.magistrate_checked_ability_to_make_state: The magistrate asked questions or otherwise checked that the injured person could make the statement.
predicates.doctor_not_examined: The doctor who was present when the statement was recorded was not examined at trial.
predicates.declaration_has_no_suspicious_features: The declaration contained relevant details and the court found no feature that cast suspicion on its credibility.
predicates.declaration_omits_accused_injury: The dying declaration did not refer to an injury sustained by the accused.
predicates.declarant_could_not_observe_accused_inju: The circumstances did not give the injured person an opportunity to observe the accused’s injury.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a conviction based on a magistrate-recorded dying declaration, the magistrate checked the declarant’s ability to speak, the declaration has no suspicious features, and an omitted injury was not observable by the declarant, the declaration may alone support the conviction even if the doctor present was not examined.

issues.legal_issue: An accused cannot establish a right of private defence merely from an injury where the evidence does not support a reasonable apprehension of danger and instead shows that the accused attacked an unarmed person.
material_facts: The dying declaration described the accused fetching a spear from his house and attacking the unarmed deceased.
The accused had a sutured injury to his lip and chin, but the evidence did not establish that the deceased had caused it; the timing and cause of the missing or loose teeth were also uncertain.
The Court considered that the lip injury could have resulted when the accused fell during the deceased’s resistance.
The evidence did not show that the accused had a reasonable apprehension of danger to his life from the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not support an inference that the accused acted in private defence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the claim of private defence against the circumstances shown by the evidence, including who initiated the attack and whether there was a reasonable apprehension of danger. It relied on no cited provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.private_defence_issue_in_criminal_convic: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction in which the accused’s claim of private defence is considered.
predicates.accused_initiated_attack_on_unarmed_pers: The evidence shows that the accused initiated an attack on an unarmed person.
predicates.accused_fetched_dangerous_weapon: The accused obtained a dangerous weapon before carrying out the attack.
predicates.accused_injury_not_linked_to_victim_atta: The evidence does not establish that the victim caused the accused’s injury during an attack by the victim.
predicates.no_evidence_of_reasonable_apprehension_o: The evidence does not show that the accused reasonably apprehended danger from the victim.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a criminal conviction, initiated an armed attack on an unarmed person, and the injury and other evidence do not show a reasonable apprehension of danger, private defence is not established.

issues.legal_issue: An intentional infliction of injuries likely to cause death, without proof that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death or that the accused intended to kill, warrants conviction for culpable homicide rather than murder.
material_facts: The attack followed a petty quarrel, and the accused fetched a weapon and inflicted several injuries on the deceased.
The accused stopped the attack after his wife intervened and allowed her to take the weapon.
The deceased died about a week later from septicemia arising from infection of the wounds.

The medical evidence did not establish with certainty that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; the evidence also left open that the gall bladder injuries could have occurred from a fall or forceful impact.
The nature of the injuries and the medical evidence showed that the injuries were likely to cause death, and the Court found that the accused intended to inflict them.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for murder was modified to conviction under Section 304 Part I IPC because the accused intended to cause the injuries but the evidence did not establish the required ordinary-course sufficiency for murder.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 300, clause thirdly, IPC, including its objective test of whether the bodily injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and Section 304 Part I IPC. It distinguished an intention to cause death or an injury meeting that objective test from an intention to cause injuries that were likely to cause death. No earlier case was cited for this classification.

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.
predicates.attack_followed_sudden_petty_quarrel: The attack followed a sudden quarrel over a petty matter.
predicates.accused_intended_to_inflict_injuries: The evidence shows that the accused intended to cause the bodily injuries inflicted.
predicates.injuries_likely_to_cause_death: The nature of the injuries and medical evidence indicate that they were likely to cause death.
predicates.ordinary_course_fatality_not_established: The evidence does not establish that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
predicates.evidence_did_not_establish_intent_to_kil: The evidence does not establish an intention to put an end to the victim’s life.
predicates.attack_stopped_when_interrupted: The accused stopped the attack when another person intervened.

issues.definition: When a murder conviction appeal involves intended injuries likely to cause death, but the evidence establishes neither ordinary-course fatality nor an intent to kill, and the attack followed a sudden petty quarrel and stopped on intervention, the conviction should be for intentional culpable homicide rather than murder.
